findings.title: Guidance as forecast and feedback
findings.claim: The Book's decree for Israel places corruption, recurrence, dispatched agents, reversal, and conditional return in an inspectable sequence; huda can therefore orient the reader to likely courses and consequences, not only name a destination.
findings.mechanism: The phrase 'in the Book' in 17:4 puts two named corruptions and their recurrence beside the focus Book; 17:5-6 narrate dispatch and reversal, while 17:8 gives a return-conditioned sequence. findings.reader_payoff: Guidance can include recognizing recurring failure and consequence while leaving room for response and return.
findings.containment: The sequence may be read as historical prediction alone. Nothing here claims that huda itself predicts these events, that the cycle mechanically determines conduct, or that proximate agents replace the ultimate governor.

findings.title: Guidance as desire correction
findings.claim: The paired call for harm and good in 17:11, followed by the description of haste, permits a bounded reading in which huda corrects what one desires before reliance is installed.
findings.mechanism: Formally parallel calls place a harmful object beside a beneficial one, and the closing haste diagnosis explains how discrimination can collapse. findings.reader_payoff: Guidance may concern not only choosing a route after desire forms, but also examining the end one is about to seek.
findings.containment: This is an exploratory, multi-step analogy. 17:11 directly diagnoses impulsive calling; it does not explicitly mention huda, wakil, or prescribe a remedy. A live alternative is that it concerns prayer alone.

findings.title: Public guidance and personal audit
findings.claim: The focus Book's public guidance and refusal of a non-divine trustee can be read alongside 17:13-17's attached, opened, and personally read account: instruction and audit meet at answerability, but a proxy cannot absorb the person's burden.
findings.mechanism: The focus Book supplies the public written standard and wakil names delegated responsibility. Later, a personal record is bound to its subject, opened for reading, and sufficient for self-accounting, while 17:15 denies transfer of a burden. Command and judgment in 17:16-17 complete the contact, turning the weak Book parallel into a bounded claim about answerability rather than textual identity.
findings.reader_payoff: The communal standard and personal account become distinct sides of answerability: guidance is public, but the subject must face their own readable record.
findings.containment: This is exploratory and the packet's connection is expressly tenuous. The two Books may remain separate motifs; only the explicit nontransferable-burden statement supports the limit on proxy accountability. No claim is made that wakil means moral liability.

findings.title: Provision does not certify direction
findings.claim: Because 17:20 extends provision to both opposed groups and says the gift is not withheld before 17:21 distinguishes their degrees, receiving provision does not by itself certify a recipient's direction or validate a chosen wakil.
findings.mechanism: The focus joins a divine gift, guidance, and a ban on substitute reliance. In 17:18-19 the immediate and later horizons diverge; 17:20 extends provision to both without restriction, and 17:21 then names unequal degrees. That sequence makes material receipt underdetermine the direction for which huda is needed.
findings.reader_payoff: A favorable circumstance cannot by itself prove that the recipient's chosen course or source of reliance is endorsed.
findings.containment: The passage may simply emphasize divine generosity. It does not call provision deceptive or explicitly mention wakil; the inference about reliance remains secondary and qualified.

findings.title: Wakil and rival ultimate reliance
findings.claim: The paired prohibitions in 17:2 and 17:22 let wakil resonate beyond an ordinary representative toward a rival center of ultimate reliance, whose promised security ends in blame and abandonment.
findings.mechanism: The focus forbids deliberately taking a trustee apart from God; 17:22 prohibits installing another deity beside God and names immobilization, blame, and abandonment. Their shared exclusivity and installation structure recasts proxy-taking as a possible rival locus of dependence, while the consequences expose its failure.
findings.reader_payoff: The ban can be heard as guarding the ultimate direction of reliance, not only as a restriction on appointing a practical agent.
findings.containment: The commands may target distinct errors: practical reliance in 17:2 and worship in 17:22. The second ayah does not lexically define wakil, and the broader dependence reading remains qualified.

epistemic.reason: The HFT support is legacy_unbound. Its exact packet coordinates agree, so the relation is retained as attributed contextual evidence; the stated alternative and boundary limit its force.

findings.title: Guidance petitioned, reliance enacted
findings.claim: The supplied Fatiha overlay adds a first-person prayer dimension to 17:2: guidance assigned to Israel is also guidance a community asks God to provide, while exclusive help-seeking enacts the refusal of another wakil.
findings.mechanism: In 1:6 the h-d-y imperative asks for guidance to the straight path; in 1:5 the community addresses God alone in worship and asks help from Him alone. These separate context acts return to focus huda and wakil, shifting the focus from a stated gift/prohibition toward petitioned direction and enacted exclusive reliance.
findings.reader_payoff: Guidance becomes perceptible both as something given and as something continually sought; the wakil prohibition is paired with an actual posture of asking God alone.
findings.containment: This is a local overlay, not an identity of wording or textual moment. 1:5 speaks of worship and help, not wakil; 1:6 names the straight path but not Moses, the Book, or Bani Israel. The help-seeking contact is analogical.

epistemic.reason: The supplied 1:6 occurrence repeats the guidance root and 1:5 directly addresses worship and help to God alone; the link to wakil is analogical, and no trust label is attached to these context projections.
